e-14402.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function
e-14402.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^3+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac 1 3 \textrm{d}u = x^2 \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot \,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-14403.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions
e-14403.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
}
$$

e-14404.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u = e^{2x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u = e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{e}^{2x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that $e^{2x} + 1 > 0$ for all $x.$

e-14407.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=-2x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-4x
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
-4 \, \textrm{d}u=16x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt {\ln 4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-2\ln 4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}16x{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\cdot 16x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-4({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-4(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\  & =4(\frac{15}{16}) \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=5-2{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\cdot 6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=5-2{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\cdot 6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=3x^3+1. Then du=9x^2 dx, so 3x^2 dx=du/3. Thus the integral is (1/3)e^u+C=(1/3)e^{3x^3+1}+C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{3}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing the Exponential Function
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{3}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 8{x}^{3}{e}^{4-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{4-{x}^{4}}\cdot 8{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-2{e}^{4-{x}^{4}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=2{x}^{2}-x.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x-1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(4x-1)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4x-1){e}^{2{x}^{2}-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{2{x}^{2}-x}\cdot (4x-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{2{x}^{2}-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={z}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2z\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=z\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int {e}^{{z}^{2}}\cdot z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{z}^{2}}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={z}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2z\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=z\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int {e}^{{z}^{2}}\cdot z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{z}^{2}}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^2/3, so du=(2x/3) dx and x dx=(3/2)du. Since ∫5^u du=5^u/ln(5), the result is 3·5^{x^2/3}/(2ln(5))+C.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}x\,⟹\,\frac{3}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{5}^{{x}^{2}/3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {5}^{{x}^{2}/3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {5}^{u}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {5}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\frac{{5}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {5}^{{x}^{2}/3}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Calculate the integral ∫x5x2/3dx.

a
5x/3ln⁡5+C
b
3⋅5x2/3ln⁡5+C
c
5x2/32+C
d
5x2/3ln⁡5+C
e
3⋅5x2/32ln⁡5+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=x23. Differentiating gives dudx=23x⟹32du=xdx.

Therefore,

∫x5x2/3dx=∫5x2/3⋅xdx=∫5u⋅32du=32∫5udu=325uln⁡5+C=3⋅5x2/32ln⁡5+C.

content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}x\,⟹\,\frac{3}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{5}^{{x}^{2}/3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {5}^{{x}^{2}/3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {5}^{u}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {5}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\frac{{5}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {5}^{{x}^{2}/3}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the integral ∫2x6x2+1dx.

a
6x2+16+C
b
6x2+1ln⁡63+C
c
6x2+1ln⁡3+C
d
6x2+1ln⁡6+C
e
6x2+1+C

decision.explanation: Let u=x^2+1, so du=2x dx. Then ∫6^u du=6^u/ln(6)+C, giving 6^{x^2+1}/ln(6)+C.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{6}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {6}^{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {6}^{u}\cdot \,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{6}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C \\  & =\frac{{6}^{{x}^{2}+1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{6}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {6}^{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {6}^{u}\cdot \,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{6}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C \\  & =\frac{{6}^{{x}^{2}+1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the integral ∫4x44x2−3dx.

a
44x2−3ln⁡4+C
b
2⋅44x2−3ln⁡4+C
c
44x2−34ln⁡4+C
d
44x2−3+C

decision.explanation: Let u=4x^2-3, so du=8x dx and 4x dx=du/2. The integral is therefore 4^u/(2ln(4))+C=4^{4x^2-3}/(2ln(4))+C.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=4{x}^{2}-3.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x\,{4}^{4{x}^{2}-3}\,\text{d}x & =4\int {4}^{4{x}^{2}-3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int {4}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{4}^{u}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =\frac{{4}^{4{x}^{2}-3}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=4x2−3. Differentiating gives dudx=8x⟹18du=xdx.

Therefore,

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=4{x}^{2}-3.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x\,{4}^{4{x}^{2}-3}\,\text{d}x & =4\int {4}^{4{x}^{2}-3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int {4}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{4}^{u}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =\frac{{4}^{4{x}^{2}-3}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$

EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=3x2. Differentiating gives dudx=6x⟹16du=xdx.

Therefore,

∫x83x2dx=∫83x2⋅xdx=∫8u⋅16du=16∫8udu=168uln⁡8+C=83x26ln⁡8+C.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option e. With u=3x^2, du=6x dx, the integral is 8^{3x^2}/(6ln(8))+C. Differentiating this result gives x8^{3x^2}, the original integrand.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{8}^{3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {8}^{3{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {8}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {8}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\frac{{8}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C \\  & =\frac{{8}^{3{x}^{2}}}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^3/5, so du=(3/5)x^2 dx. Thus the integral is (5/3)∫4^u du=5·4^{x^3/5}/(3ln(4))+C.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=\frac{{x}^{3}}{5}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{5}{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{5}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{4}^{{x}^{3}/5}\,\text{d}x & =\int {4}^{{x}^{3}/5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {4}^{u}\cdot \frac{5}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int {4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5\cdot {4}^{u}}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =\frac{5\cdot {4}^{{x}^{3}/5}}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

c
4x3/53+C
d
3⋅4x3/55ln⁡4+C

4x3ln⁡4+C

Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=x35. Differentiating gives dudx=35x2⟹53du=x2dx.

Therefore,

∫x24x3/5dx=∫4x3/5⋅x2dx=∫4u⋅53du=53∫4udu=5⋅4u3ln⁡4+C=5⋅4x3/53ln⁡4+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Other Exponential Functions
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=\frac{{x}^{3}}{5}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{5}{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{5}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{4}^{{x}^{3}/5}\,\text{d}x & =\int {4}^{{x}^{3}/5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {4}^{u}\cdot \frac{5}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int {4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5\cdot {4}^{u}}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =\frac{5\cdot {4}^{{x}^{3}/5}}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 11
?

Calculate the integral ∫5x5x+1dx.

a
5xln⁡5+C
b
15xln⁡5+C
c
ln⁡(5x+1)5ln⁡5+C
d
ln⁡(5x+1)ln⁡5+C
e
5ln⁡(5x+1)ln⁡5+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=5^x+1, so du=5^x ln(5) dx. The integral is ln(u)/ln(5)+C. Since 5^x+1>0, this gives ln(5^x+1)/ln(5)+C.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u={5}^{x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u={5}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{{5}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{5}^{x}+1}\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|{5}^{x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that ${5}^{x}+1>0$ for all $x.$

Question 11
?

Calculate the integral ∫5x5x+1dx.

a
5xln⁡5+C
b
15xln⁡5+C
c
ln⁡(5x+1)5ln⁡5+C
d
ln⁡(5x+1)ln⁡5+C
e
5ln⁡(5x+1)ln⁡5+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable u=5x+1. Differentiating gives

dudx=5xln⁡5⟹1ln⁡5du=5xdx.

Therefore,

∫5x5x+1dx=∫15x+1⋅5xdx=∫1u⋅1ln⁡5du=1ln⁡5∫1udu=1ln⁡5⋅ln⁡|u|+C=1ln⁡5⋅ln⁡|5x+1|+C=ln⁡(5x+1)ln⁡5+C.

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that 5x+1>0 for all x.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. Substituting u=5^x+1 gives du=5^x ln(5) dx, yielding ln(5^x+1)/ln(5)+C. Its derivative is 5^x/(5^x+1), verifying the result.

content.knowledge_point: More Complex Cases
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u={5}^{x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u={5}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{{5}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{5}^{x}+1}\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|{5}^{x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that ${5}^{x}+1>0$ for all $x.$

Question 13
?

Calculate the integral ∫4x4x+2dx.

a
4ln⁡(4x+2)ln⁡4+C
b
ln⁡(4x+2)ln⁡4+C
c
14xln⁡4+C
d
ln⁡(4x)ln⁡4+C
e
ln⁡(4x+2)4ln⁡4+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=4^x+2, so du=4^x ln(4) dx. The integral becomes ln(u)/ln(4)+C. Since 4^x+2>0, the answer is ln(4^x+2)/ln(4)+C.

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u={4}^{x}+2.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}u={4}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{4}^{x}}{{4}^{x}+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{4}^{x}+2}\cdot {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|{4}^{x}+2|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x}+2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that ${4}^{x}+2>0$ for all $x.$

$$

Question 14
?

Calculate the integral ∫2x+12x−5dx.

a
23ln⁡22x−5+C
b
23(2x−5)3+C
c
22x−5+C
d
 6ln⁡2(2x−5)3+C
e
43ln⁡2(2x−5)3+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=2^x-5, so du=2^x ln(2) dx. Since 2^{x+1}=2·2^x, the integral becomes (2/ln(2))∫u^{1/2} du=4u^{3/2}/(3ln(2))+C, matching option e.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={2}^{x}-5.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & ={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}u={2}^{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {2}^{x+1}\sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\cdot {2}^{x}\sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\cdot {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{({2}^{x}-5)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Calculate the integral ∫2x+12x−5dx.

a
23ln⁡22x−5+C
b
23(2x−5)3+C
c
22x−5+C
d
 6ln⁡2(2x−5)3+C
e
43ln⁡2(2x−5)3+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=2x−5. Differentiating gives

dudx=2xln⁡2⟹1ln⁡2du=2xdx.

Therefore,

∫2x+12x−5dx=∫2⋅2x2x−5dx=2∫2x−5⋅2xdx=2∫u⋅1ln⁡2du=2ln⁡2∫u1/2du=2ln⁡2⋅u3/2(32)+C=2ln⁡2⋅23⋅u3/2=43ln⁡2u3+C=43ln⁡2(2x−5)3+C.

content.knowledge_point: More Complex Cases
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={2}^{x}-5.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & ={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}u={2}^{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {2}^{x+1}\sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\cdot {2}^{x}\sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \sqrt{{2}^{x}-5}\cdot {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{({2}^{x}-5)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

103(ex+4)3+C
b

e

decision.explanation: Let u=e^x+4, so du=e^x dx. The integral becomes 5∫u^{1/2} du=(10/3)u^{3/2}+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={e}^{x}+4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u={e}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int 5{e}^{x}\sqrt{{e}^{x}+4}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \sqrt{{e}^{x}+4}\cdot {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =5\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C \\  & =\frac{10}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{10}{3}\sqrt{({e}^{x}+4)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the integral ∫0ln⁡515xe2x2dx.

a
120
b
320
c
6
d
15
e
65
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=2x2. Differentiating gives dudx=4x⟹14du=xdx.

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

x 0 ln⁡5
u 0 2ln⁡5

Therefore, we get ∫0ln⁡515xe2x2dx=15∫0ln⁡5e2x2⋅xdx=15∫02ln⁡5eu⋅14du=120∫02ln⁡5eudu=120eu|02ln⁡5=120(e2ln⁡5−e0)=120(25−1)=2420=65.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating Definite Integrals
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=2{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2\operatorname{ln}⁡5$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}}\frac{1}{5}x{e}^{2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}}{e}^{2{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{20}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{20}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}(25-1) \\  & =\frac{24}{20} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 20
after.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}x{4}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{{4}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(4-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Evaluate the integral ∫01x4x2dx.

a
3ln⁡24
b
3ln⁡2
c
43ln⁡2
d
34ln⁡2
e
4ln⁡23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's introduce the new variable u=x2. Differentiating gives dudx=2x⟹12du=xdx.

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

x 0 1
u 0 1

Therefore, we get ∫01x4x2dx=∫014x2⋅xdx=∫014u⋅12du=12∫014udu=124uln⁡4|01=12ln⁡4(4−1)=32ln⁡4=34ln⁡2.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating Definite Integrals
content.worked_solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, we determine the new limits of integration:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}x{4}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{{4}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(4-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$
